blocks.prompt: The Dolphin Is Not a Fish
blocks.text: A dolphin looks like a fish, but it is not one. A dolphin is a mammal, the same as a dog or a cow or you. Mammals breathe air. A fish can stay under the water all day. A dolphin cannot. It holds its breath, then swims up and puffs the old air out of its blowhole. You can hear the puff from far away. A baby dolphin is called a calf. The calf drinks milk from its mom and stays close to her for years. Dolphins live in groups called pods. The pod swims together, hunts together, and rests together.

blocks.prompt: Seeing in the Dark Water
blocks.text: The sea is a dark place. Sunlight reaches the top of the water and then gives up. Below that, everything turns murky and gray. A dolphin can still find one fish in all that water, and it can do it with its eyes shut. Here is how. The dolphin makes a stream of fast clicks inside its head. The clicks shoot out through its forehead and travel away through the water. When a click hits a fish, it bounces back. The dolphin hears that echo. From the echo it knows where the fish is, how big it is, and which way it is turning. Using sound this way is called echolocation. Bats do the same thing in the air at night. A dolphin can click hundreds of times a second. As it closes in, it clicks faster and faster, until the clicks blur together into a buzz. Divers who have been near a hunting dolphin say the buzz feels like a tingle on your skin. To a dolphin, sound is a way of seeing.

(inference: faster clicks give it more information, so it can track a moving fish)

4.title: The Dolphin That Sees With Sound
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Dolphin That Sees With Sound

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Sound moves about 4 times faster in water than in air
The melon is a lens made of fat
A dolphin hears through its lower jaw
Clicks are aimed in a narrow beam
Dolphins had sonar long before people built it

blocks.prompt: A Lens Made of Fat
blocks.text:
Point a flashlight into the ocean and the beam dies within a few dozen feet. Water swallows light. Sound has the opposite habit. It travels through water about four times faster than it travels through air, and it carries much further before it fades. Dolphins worked this out tens of millions of years before people built the first sonar.

A dolphin's clicks do not come from its mouth. They are made by tissue just under the blowhole, then pushed forward into a lump of fat in the forehead called the melon. The melon works like a lens, except it bends sound instead of light. By squeezing and relaxing the melon, a dolphin can shape its clicks into a narrow beam and aim it, the way you might narrow a flashlight down to a spot.

The return trip is stranger. A dolphin has ear holes, but it barely uses them. The echo comes back and passes into the thin bone of the lower jaw, which is filled with fat that carries the sound straight to the inner ear. A dolphin hears through its chin.

What comes back is not a picture the way your eyes make a picture. It is a shape built out of timing. A close echo returns sooner than a far one. A hard thing like bone returns a sharper echo than soft flesh. In tests, dolphins have found a target the size of a small orange from the length of a football field away, and they can tell one metal from another by echo alone.

answers: water swallows light, but sound travels about four times faster in water and carries much further

(inference: a nearer object returns its echo sooner, so the delays tell the dolphin the shape and distance)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Tursiops truncatus, the bottlenose dolphin
Each dolphin invents its own signature whistle
Dolphins copy each other's whistles to call them
It sleeps with one half of its brain at a time
Every breath a dolphin takes is a decision

blocks.prompt: The Name It Made Up Itself
blocks.text:
Every bottlenose dolphin has a name, and it makes the name up itself.

Within the first few months of life, a calf invents a whistle: a rising, falling, looping pattern of pure tone that belongs to no other dolphin in the sea. Biologists call it a signature whistle. The calf keeps it for the rest of its life, which can run past fifty years. When two groups of dolphins meet in open water, they trade signature whistles before anything else happens, the way strangers trade names before they trade anything worth saying.

What makes it a name rather than a badge is what the other dolphins do with it. A dolphin can copy another dolphin's signature whistle and broadcast it, and the owner of that whistle answers. Off the coast of Scotland, researchers played wild dolphins recordings of their own signature whistles, and then recordings of whistles belonging to strangers. Each dolphin replied to its own and ignored the rest. That is not a call. That is being addressed.

Sleep is the second thing dolphins do differently, and the reason is grim. A dolphin's breathing is not automatic the way yours is. Every breath is a decision it has to make. If a dolphin ever fell fully asleep the way you do, it would drown. So it sleeps with half of its brain at a time. One half powers down. The other half stays awake, keeps the body swimming slowly, and keeps watch with the eye on its side. Some hours later the two halves swap. The open eye closes and the closed eye opens.

Sit with what that means. A dolphin has never once been completely unconscious. Not in fifty years. It has never fully let go. Mothers and newborn calves go further still: for weeks after a birth, neither one seems to sleep properly at all, swimming and surfacing around the clock until the calf is strong enough to keep up with the group.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Dolphin That Sees With Sound

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Shark Bay dolphins hunt with sponges on their beaks
Sponging passes from mother to daughter
Its flipper holds the bones of a hand
Two floating bones are all that is left of its hips
Its ancestors walked on land about 50 million years ago
A dolphin must decide to take every breath

blocks.prompt: The Sponge, the Hand, and the Borrowed Lungs
blocks.text:
In Shark Bay, on the western edge of Australia, a small number of bottlenose dolphins hunt with a tool. A dolphin swims to the seafloor, tears loose a cone-shaped sponge, fits it over her beak like a glove, and goes poking through the rubble with her nose protected. The fish she wants are buried down there, and they have no swim bladder, which means they throw back a poor echo and cannot easily be found by sound. So she sets aside her best sense and feels for them instead, while the sponge takes the scrapes her skin would otherwise take.

Not every dolphin in Shark Bay does this. Roughly one in twenty does, and nearly all of them descend from a single female, nicknamed Sponging Eve, who seems to have worked it out within the last two hundred years. Daughters learn it from their mothers. Sons mostly do not. The technique travels down the female line the way a family recipe does, which is to say by watching, not by instinct and not by instruction. Scientists have a plain word for a behavior invented by an individual, spread by example, and inherited socially rather than genetically. The word is culture.

That claim used to be a fight. For most of the twentieth century, culture was treated as the wall between people and every other animal. The sponging dolphins did not knock that wall down, but they put a serious crack in it, because the pattern resists every other explanation. Spongers are not a separate species. They are not genetically special. They live in the same bay as everyone else, eating different food, using a trick some of them know and others simply do not.

The rest of the animal makes more sense once you know where it came from. Dolphins are not fish and never were. Their ancestors were four-legged land mammals that waded into the shallows around fifty million years ago and never came back out. The evidence is still in the body. Under the skin of a dolphin's flipper are the bones of a hand: an upper arm, a forearm, a wrist, and five splayed fingers. Buried in its abdomen are two small floating bones, all that survives of a pelvis that once carried hind legs. A dolphin breathes air because its ancestors breathed air, and it has never managed to stop.

That inheritance is expensive. A dolphin must decide to breathe, every single time, which is why it can only ever sleep with half its brain at once. It must reach the surface even under ice, even while being hunted, even while giving birth. Evolution did not redesign the animal from scratch when it went back to the water. It reshaped a land mammal into the outline of a fish and left the plumbing exactly where it was.

So look again at the sponger. She is a converted land animal, breathing air she has to remember to take, carrying a name she invented for herself, wearing a sponge her mother taught her to wear, hunting fish she cannot hear. Almost none of it is instinct. Almost all of it is learned. People like to ask whether dolphins are intelligent, and Shark Bay shows why that is the wrong question. The interesting thing is not how clever any single dolphin is. It is that one good idea, thought up once by one animal, is still being used two centuries later by her great-great-granddaughters, in the same bay, on the same seafloor, for the same buried fish.
